articles.excerpt: Front-end developers often end up as the unofficial "slides person" on a team. We can build a beautiful deck with HTML and CSS in an hour, but the request that follows is almost always the same: "Plea…
articles.body: Front-end developers often end up as the unofficial "slides person" on a team. We can build a beautiful deck with HTML and CSS in an hour, but the request that follows is almost always the same: "Please send it as PowerPoint." These are my notes on handling that request efficiently, from the perspective of someone who cares about clean markup. Background: why HTML decks keep appearing Three trends push presentations toward HTML: AI generation. Large language models output HTML and CSS reliably. Ask for slides and you get a single .html file. Frameworks. Reveal.js, Slidev, Marp and similar tools let developers write slides in Markdown and render them as web pages. Design systems. Teams want slides to match the product's own components, colours and typography.

articles.title: Routing Browser-Agent Workflows vs. Human SDR Handoffs: The New Speed-to-Lead Frontier
articles.excerpt: Speed-to-lead has long been a numbers game. The most-cited research is the MIT/InsideSales.com Lead Response Management Study, led by Dr. James Oldroyd. It analyzed more than 15,000 leads and 100,000…
articles.body: Speed-to-lead has long been a numbers game. The most-cited research is the MIT/InsideSales.com Lead Response Management Study, led by Dr. James Oldroyd. It analyzed more than 15,000 leads and 100,000 call attempts, and found that contacting a lead within five minutes made a team about 100 times more likely to reach that lead, and 21 times more likely to qualify it, than waiting 30 minutes. That study dates from 2007, and its figures are usually repeated through vendor summaries. Treat them as directional evidence of how fast intent decays, not as a precise forecast for your funnel. Most teams still miss the five-minute window.

articles.title: Why 90% of Open-Source Trading Bots Blow Up (And How We Engineered STRIDE with Formal Risk Bounds in Python 3.12)
articles.excerpt: If you browse GitHub for trading bots or algorithmic finance repositories, you will find thousands of projects promising automated riches. Yet, when you dive into the source code, an alarming pattern…
articles.body: If you browse GitHub for trading bots or algorithmic finance repositories, you will find thousands of projects promising automated riches. Yet, when you dive into the source code, an alarming pattern emerges. Almost without exception, retail quantitative codebases suffer from critical architectural flaws that guarantee long-term account ruin in live markets. First, unintentional look-ahead bias: inadvertently slicing time-series data such that a bar accesses prices or statistics from the future. Second, naive lot sizing: allocating 10% of equity into an asset regardless of whether its annualized volatility is 12% (like short-term bonds) or 80% (like silver, tech breakouts, or crypto).

articles.title: Your AI App Has a Rate Limit. Your Agent Can Still Run Up the Bill.
articles.excerpt: A user clicks “Research this topic.” Your app accepts one request. Behind the scenes, the agent searches the web, reads pages, calls the model, retries a failed tool, and searches again. Your rate lim…
articles.body: A user clicks “Research this topic.” Your app accepts one request. Behind the scenes, the agent searches the web, reads pages, calls the model, retries a failed tool, and searches again. Your rate limiter sees one request. Your infrastructure sees a growing chain of work. Limiting requests at the entrance doesn’t limit everything that happens afterward. If you’re building an AI feature, here’s how to keep that work under control. 1. Count the work behind the button Imagine a research task that uses: One model call to plan. Five searches. Ten page fetches. Several model calls to analyze results. One final call to write the answer. That’s an illustrative workflow, but it shows the problem: one user action can trigger many billable operations.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
articles.excerpt: Five spooky skywatching targets perfect for naked eye stargazing this Halloween!
articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.
articles.author: Anthony Wood

Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Rosetta’s Selfie Explanation: This Rosetta spacecraft selfie was snapped on October 7th, 2014. At the time the comet-chasing spacecraft was about 472 million kilometers from planet Earth, but only 16 kilometers from the surface of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko . Looming beyond the spacecraft near the top of the frame, dust and gas stream away from the comet’s curious double-lobed nucleus .
